modal-dialog.modal-heading: What’s a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

modal-content.p: An HSA is a type of savings account that lets you set aside money on a pre-tax basis to pay for qualified medical expenses.
You can use the funds in an HSA at any time to pay for qualified medical expenses. But you may contribute to an HSA only if you meet certain requirements, including that you:

ul.li: Have a High-Deductible Health Plan
Have no other health coverage except certain allowed coverage
Aren’t enrolled in Medicare
Can’t be claimed as someone else’s dependent in

modal-content.p: Refer to Publication 969, Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans for more on HSAs.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What’s a Form 1099-SA?

modal-content.p: Form 1099-SA is issued by Health Savings Account (HSA) trustees, like banks or insurance companies, to report distribution amounts made that year from an HSA to pay for qualified medical expenses.
Depending on who issued it, Forms 1099-SA may look different, but they should all have the name "Distributions From an HSA, Archer MSA, or Medicare Advantage MSA" on the form.
Usually, taxpayers who have taken a distribution in get a Form 1099-SA by January 31, .
Even if you didn’t get a Form 1099-SA, you’re still required to report any distributions taken from an HSA on your federal tax return.

p.strong: What if I’m missing a Form 1099-SA?

modal-content.p: If you lost or never received your Form 1099-SA, ask your HSA trustee for a copy.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are qualified medical expenses for a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

modal-content.p: Generally, qualified medical expenses for HSA purposes are medical expenses that weren’t covered by an insurance plan. They include many types of medical expenses (outlined in more detail in Publication 502, Medical and Dental Expenses), as well as some general health expenses such as:

ul.li: Nonprescription medication
Menstrual care products, like tampons and pads
Personal protective equipment, such as masks and hand sanitizer, to prevent the spread of COVID-19
Home testing for COVID-19

modal-content.p: In order to qualify, medical expenses must be taken after an HSA was established.
Refer to Publication 969, Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans for more on qualified medical expenses.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What Health Savings Account (HSA) situations aren’t yet supported in Direct File?

modal-content.p: Direct File only supports simple HSA situations.
It doesn’t support:

ul.li: Changes in marital status or coverage that affect your contribution limit. This includes getting married, not being covered by a High-Deductible Health Plan all year, or switching between self-only and family plans
Situations where you owe additional tax. This includes excess (extra) contributions, even if they’re withdrawn before
Situations where the HSA contributions listed on Form W-2 aren’t the total employer contributions for . For example, if additional contributions are being made through an employer in for
Situations where you have additional income. This includes distributions that aren’t for qualified medical expenses
Lump sum distributions from an HSA you inherited from someone who died. If this situation applies, Form 1099-SA will have a value in box 4 and code 4 or 6 in box 3
Archer or Medicare Advantage Medical Savings Accounts (MSAs). These accounts are reported on the same income tax form as HSAs but are different

modal-content.p: These situations require filing additional forms or worksheets that Direct File doesn’t currently support.
If any of these unsupported situations apply to you, you’ll need to file using another tool. Find other ways to file your taxes.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What is a Health Savings Account (HSA) rollover or a trustee-to-trustee transfer?

modal-content.p: A rollover is a tax-free distribution (withdrawal) of funds from one HSA that is reinvested into another HSA of the same account beneficiary. Generally, you must complete the rollover within 60 days after you received the distribution. An HSA can only receive one rollover contribution during a 1-year period.

In a trustee-to-trustee transfer, you instruct the trustee of your HSA to transfer funds directly to the trustee of another of your HSAs. This transfer isn’t considered a rollover. There is no limit on the number of these transfers.
Rollovers and trustee-to-trustee transfers aren’t included in your income, aren’t eligible for the HSA deduction, and don’t reduce your contribution limit.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Where can I find Health Savings Account (HSA) contribution information?

modal-content.p: HSA trustees, like banks or insurance companies, issue Form 5498-SA to report the yearly status of an HSA. This form includes the total contribution amount for the year. Since you can make contributions to an HSA for up until , this form could be sent as late as .
If you haven’t received Form 5498-SA yet, check your HSA monthly statements or reach out to the HSA trustee for this information.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What is a Health Savings Account (HSA) rollover or a trustee-to-trustee transfer?

modal-content.p: A rollover is a tax-free distribution (withdrawal) of funds from one HSA that is reinvested into another HSA of the same account beneficiary. Generally, you must complete the rollover within 60 days after you received the distribution. An HSA can only receive one rollover contribution during a 1-year period.

In a trustee-to-trustee transfer, you instruct the trustee of your HSA to transfer funds directly to the trustee of another of your HSAs. This transfer isn’t considered a rollover. There is no limit on the number of these transfers.
Rollovers and trustee-to-trustee transfers aren’t included in your income, aren’t eligible for the HSA deduction, and don’t reduce your contribution limit.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What makes someone eligible to contribute to a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

modal-content.p: To be an eligible individual and qualify to make HSA contributions, you must meet the following requirements:

ul.li: You are covered under a High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) on the first day of the month
You have no other health coverage except certain allowed coverage
You aren’t enrolled in Medicare
You can’t be claimed as a dependent on someone else’s tax return

Allowed health coverage

ul.li: Accidents
Disability
Dental care
Vision care
Long-term care
Telehealth and other remote care

modal-content.p: For a complete list of allowed coverage, refer to Publication 969, Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans..

Which months you were considered eligible. You’re considered having HDHP coverage for all of a month if you had coverage on the first day of the month

modal-dialog.modal-heading: When can spouses split their contribution limit between their separate Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)?

modal-content.p: Spouses are allowed to split their contribution amounts between their HSAs however they like if they meet all of the following conditions:

ul.li: Each have separate HSAs
Each are eligible to contribute to their HSA
At least 1 has family coverage under their High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP)

modal-content.p: For example, spouses could choose to allocate 50% of their contributions to each spouse’s accounts or 100% to 1 spouse’s account.

p.strong: Changes in marital status or coverage

modal-content.p: If spouses only meet these conditions for part of the year (due to marriage, divorce, or changes in coverage), they’re still allowed to allocate their contributions for the months when the conditions applied. However, Direct File doesn’t yet support this situation.
Refer to Instructions for Form 8889 for more information about allocations.

An HSA can be used to pay for the qualified medical expenses of multiple people. However, you can’t have a joint account with multiple owners.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What is a Health Savings Account (HSA) rollover or a trustee-to-trustee transfer?

modal-content.p: A rollover is a tax-free distribution (withdrawal) of funds from one HSA that is reinvested into another HSA of the same account beneficiary. Generally, you must complete the rollover within 60 days after you received the distribution. An HSA can only receive one rollover contribution during a 1-year period.

In a trustee-to-trustee transfer, you instruct the trustee of your HSA to transfer funds directly to the trustee of another of your HSAs. This transfer isn’t considered a rollover. There is no limit on the number of these transfers.
Rollovers and trustee-to-trustee transfers aren’t included in your income, aren’t eligible for the HSA deduction, and don’t reduce your contribution limit.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are excess (extra) contributions to Health Savings Accounts (HSAs)?

modal-content.p: Excess contributions are any contribution amount over the HSA contribution limit.

If you’ve contributed over the limit, there’s a 6% penalty for each year that the excess contributions remain in the HSA. To avoid having excess contributions for and paying a penalty, you can withdraw them before . If you leave any excess contributions in the HSA, then you’ll owe the penalty.

Direct File doesn’t yet support excess contributions, even if they’re withdrawn before . If you had excess contributions in an HSA at any point in , you’ll need to file using another tool. Find other ways to file your taxes.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What is the last-month rule for Health Savings Account (HSA) contributions?

modal-content.p: If you weren’t eligible to contribute all year to an HSA, the last-month rule is an alternative way to calculate the HSA contribution limit.
The last-month rule allows you to contribute to an HSA as if you had been eligible all year if:

ul.li: You’re eligible on the first day of the last month of your tax year (for example, December 1, )
You remain eligible throughout the next year (for example, December 1, –December 31, )

p.strong: What happens if I used the last-month rule in but didn’t remain eligible to contribute to an HSA in ?

modal-content.p: If you used the last-month rule to calculate the contribution limit in and then didn’t remain eligible for all 12 months of , you may have additional income to report in . Direct File doesn’t yet support this situation. You will need to find another filing tool.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What makes someone eligible to contribute to a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

modal-content.p: To be an eligible individual and qualify to make HSA contributions, you must meet the following requirements:

ul.li: You are covered under a High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) on the first day of the month
You have no other health coverage except certain allowed coverage
You aren’t enrolled in Medicare
You can’t be claimed as a dependent on someone else’s tax return

modal-content.p:
Allowed health coverage
</br>If you (and your spouse, if you have family coverage) have HDHP coverage, you can’t generally have any other health coverage. However, some other types of coverage are allowed, including:

ul.li: Accidents
Disability
Dental care
Vision care
Long-term care
Telehealth and other remote care

modal-content.p: For a complete list of allowed coverage, refer to Publication 969, Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans..

modal-content.p: The maximum amount that can be contributed to an HSA depends on:

ul.li: The type of High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) coverage you have. For , if you have self-only coverage, your maximum contribution is . If you have family coverage, your maximum contribution is
Which months you were considered eligible. You’re considered having HDHP coverage for all of a month if you had coverage on the first day of the month
Your age. If you’re age 55 or older at the end of , the contribution limit is increased by for your HSA

modal-dialog.modal-heading: When can I take distributions from a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

modal-content.p: While you’re only allowed to contribute to an HSA if you meet certain requirements, you can take a distribution of the funds in an HSA at any time to pay for qualified medical expenses.

p.strong: Distributions not used for qualified medical expenses.

modal-content.p: Any distributions not used for qualified medical expenses are subject to an additional 20% tax. The additional 20% tax doesn’t apply to distributions made after the account beneficiary:

ul.li: Dies
Becomes disabled
Turns age 65.

modal-content.p: Direct File doesn’t yet support distributions that weren’t used for qualified medical expenses.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What Health Savings Account (HSA) distributions aren’t yet supported in Direct File?

modal-content.p: Direct File currently supports distributions on Form 1099-SA that have code 1 (normal distributions) in box 3
You can’t yet use Direct File to report:

ul.li: Forms 1099-SAs with codes 2-6 in box 3
Distributions that weren’t used for qualified medical expenses.
Excess (extra) contributions withdrawn before .

modal-content.p: If you received distributions not yet supported by Direct File, you’ll need to file using another tool. Find other ways to file your taxes.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: How are taxable Health Savings Account (HSA) distributions calculated?

modal-content.p: Distributions used for qualified medical expenses aren’t taxable. If the amount of distributions (box 1 minus any rollovers or withdrawn excess contributions) is equal to the amount of qualified medical expenses, then the taxable distribution amount is $0.

If the amount of distributions is greater than the amount of qualified medical expenses, then this extra amount is taxable income. An additional 20% tax is applied, unless the distributions were made after the account beneficiary:

ul.li: Died
Became disabled
Turned age 65

modal-content.p: Direct File doesn’t yet support taxable HSA distributions.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Where do I find information about excess contributions withdrawn before ?

modal-content.p: This information isn’t marked on Form 1099-SA. Check your Health Savings Account monthly statements for the excess (extra) contributions that were withdrawn.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Why do we ask about fair market value (FMV) and date of death?

modal-content.p: FMV refers to the value of a plan’s assets on a particular date.
If a Health Savings Account (HSA) is held by someone who dies and the designated beneficiary isn’t the surviving spouse, then the account:

ul.li: Ceases to be an HSA on the account holder’s death
Has its FMV calculated based on the account holder’s date of death
Has its balance distributed to the designated beneficiary as taxable income but without the additional 20% tax for distributions that aren’t for qualified medical expenses.

modal-content.p: Direct File doesn’t yet support this situation.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are qualified medical expenses for a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

modal-content.p: Generally, qualified medical expenses for HSA purposes are medical expenses that weren’t covered by an insurance plan. They include many types of medical expenses (outlined in more detail in Publication 502, Medical and Dental Expenses), as well as some general health expenses such as:

ul.li: Nonprescription medication
Menstrual care products, like tampons and pads
Personal protective equipment, such as masks and hand sanitizer, to prevent the spread of COVID-19
Home testing for COVID-19

modal-content.p: In order to qualify, medical expenses must be taken after an HSA was established.
Refer to Publication 969, Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans for more on qualified medical expenses.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Where do I find the total amount of qualified medical expenses paid using distributions from a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

modal-content.p: The amount isn’t on Form 1099-SA.
Individual amounts can often be found on:

ul.li: Explanations of Benefits from your insurance company
Receipts

modal-content.p: The IRS generally recommends keeping an itemized list of these expenses in your records for 3 to 6 years.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Whose medical expenses can be covered by Health Savings Account (HSA) distributions?

modal-content.p: If you have a self-only plan, include medical expenses for yourself.
If you have a family plan, include medical expenses for yourself, your spouse, and your dependents.
If you have a family plan, you can also include medical expenses from these situations:

ul.li:
Any medical expenses that you paid for any person who would have been considered your dependent except that:
They filed a joint return
They had gross income
You, or your spouse if filing jointly, are dependents of someone else

Parents who are divorced, separated, or living apart for the last 6 months of the calendar year can treat their child (or children) as the dependent of both parents, whether or not the custodial parent releases claim to the child as the custodial parent’s dependent.
In this situation, either parent can cover qualified medical expenses for the child with HSA distributions.
